newsitem.title: CROATIA: Election to be held despite Serb boycott threat-UN.
newsitem.headline: Election to be held despite Serb boycott threat-UN.

text.p: The United Nations stressed on Monday that a crucial postwar election in Croatia's last Serb enclave Eastern Slavonia will be held despite Serb hardliners' hint of a boycott call following an informal referendum.

Sunday's referendum was staged to decide whether Eastern Slavonia should be a single administrative unit, ahead of April 13 elections which will pave the way for the enclave's reintegration with Croatia, ending six years of rebellion.

The Yugoslav news agency Tanjug said 99 percent of those who voted on Sunday opted for the region not to be divided in two units, as it was in pre-1991 Croatia, which would reduce Serb chances of retaining majority control of the area.

"We have told (the Serbs) in every possible way that the referendum is not binding or valid, that the election is taking place anyway and that it is a crucial vote for them," U.N. spokesman Philip Arnold told Reuters.

He was unable to confirm Serb media reports of a turnout of over 70 percent but hinted the figures may not be reliable as "some observers noted that some people who went into voting areas were not checked for identification".

About half of some 120,000 Serbs now in the area are refugees from other enclaves. There are also over 80,000 Croatian refugees, expelled from the region in 1991, who are more than keen to reclaim their property.

Serbs united in a single party bloc to avoid dispersion of votes started a low-key last-minute electoral campaign last Thursday, aimed at winning from Croatian parties a dozen of some 30 municipalities at stake.

But Tanjug said the regional Serb council, a relic of the old rebel administration that lacks executive power but retains some influence, would convene on Tuesday to reach a "definite" decision whether the Serbs should vote at all on Sunday.
Arnold said the council would only "recommend", not decide. "They know the election will be held," he said.
UNTAES once again moved the deadline for registering all voters from last Friday to this Tuesday evening because "we wanted to give everybody a possibility to vote", said Arnold.
More than 140,000 people, including original Croat and Serb residents, had registered to vote so far. "The majority of those are in the region," Arnold said.
He had no breakdown on the number of Serbs registered. However, more than half of the Serb population has obtained Croatian citizenship papers which would qualify them to vote.

Eastern Slavonia, a fertile, oil-producing strip on the Danube River border with Serbia, was one of three regions that rebelled against Croatia's secession from federal Yugoslavia in 1991 and proclaimed their own Serb state.
Croatia recaptured two of the enclaves two years ago, prompting Serbs in Eastern Slavonia to sign an agreement accepting a gradual, peaceful return to Croatian rule.

The area is now administered and monitored by some 5,000 U.N. peacekeepers (UNTAES) who will start to leave after their mandate expires on July 15, simultaneously with the reintroduction of Croatian rule.
